assertions.value: The paper defines an ε-coreset: for a set of points P and a monotone measure function f, a subset Q of P is an ε-coreset of P if |f(Q) − f(P)| ≤ ε · f(P).
quotes: Definition 1. (Coreset) Let P be a set of points in space V, and f be a monotone measure function, we call a subset Q ⊆ P as an ε-coreset of P , if |f (Q) − f (P )| ≤ ε · f (P ). (3)

assertions.value: The authors construct the coreset as a k-center problem: choose k centers so that the maximum distance from any point to its nearest center (the radius δc) is minimized. They state this is NP-hard, but a provable greedy algorithm efficiently finds a 2-approximate solution.

papers.what_it_is: A Google Quantum AI paper that defines generative quantum advantage, proves classical hardness and quantum easiness for learning shallow generative QNNs and for compressing circuits, and reports experiments on a 68-qubit superconducting processor.

existing.note: The informal Theorem 1 is made formal as Theorems 12 and 13 in Appendix H.3. Both rest on Conjecture 1, which Proposition 4 derives from the assumption that the non-uniform polynomial hierarchy does not collapse. The proof covers exact sampling; approximate sampling relies on counting-problem results from cited work.
existing.value: The paper proves (Theorems 12 and 13) that learning generative tomographically-complete shallow QNNs and generative instantaneously-deep QNNs is quantumly easy but classically hard under Conjecture 1, and proves (Proposition 4) that Conjecture 1 holds if the non-uniform polynomial hierarchy does not collapse. The authors state that the result covers exact sampling, and that extending it to approximate sampling relies on the classical hardness of some counting problems from cited work.

Theorem 13 (Generative advantage with instantaneously-deep QNNs). Learning generative instantaneously-deep QNNs is quantumly easy but classically hard under Conjecture 1.
Proposition 4. Assuming the non-uniform polynomial hierarchy does not collapse, Conjecture 1 is true.
